lead: Today the Church tells two stories of towns and people who were given a great gift. In Exodus a baby is drawn out of the Nile by an Egyptian princess, and grows up to be the one who will draw Israel out of Egypt. In the Gospel Jesus speaks sorrowfully to the Galilean towns of Chorazin, Bethsaida and Capernaum, where he did most of his mighty works, because they did not change their hearts. The first reading shows how God quietly saves; the Gospel shows how much is asked of those who have seen his work. Today the Church also remembers St Henry, the emperor who ruled in the early eleventh century and died in 1024; the Mass of the weekday is kept.

set: The book of Exodus opens with the Israelites multiplying in Egypt and with a king who feared them. Pharaoh set them to forced labor (1:11–14) and then ordered that every Hebrew boy be thrown into the Nile (1:22). Chapter 2 begins with a family from the tribe of Levi who will not obey that decree. Their names are not given here; the Bible names them later as Amram and Jochebed (6:20).
str: vv. 1–4: a Levite mother hides her son for three months, then places him in a basket among the reeds, with his sister watching.
vv. 5–10: Pharaoh’s daughter finds him, takes pity, and unknowingly hires his own mother as his nurse; she names him Moses.
vv. 11–15a: the grown Moses sees the forced labor of his people, kills an Egyptian, and flees from Pharaoh to Midian.
kw: The same rare word is used for Noah’s ark (Genesis 6:14). In both stories a vessel of wood or reed carries life safely through the waters of death.
The mother “saw that he was a fine baby”. The Hebrew is the word of Genesis 1, “God saw that it was good”. A quiet echo of creation: a new life, a new beginning.

The name sounds like the Hebrew verb māšâ, “to draw out”, which the princess uses in her explanation. Many scholars note that the name may also be Egyptian, meaning “born of” as in the name Thutmose. Either way, the story says that this child is the one who will draw out a people.
vv: when she saw that he was a fine baby, she hid him three months.
The parents act in faith. The Letter to the Hebrews says that it was by faith that Moses was hidden by his parents, because they were not afraid of the king’s edict (Hebrews 11:23).
He was crying, and she took pity on him.

The one who saves the child is not an Israelite but a daughter of the very house that threatens him. God works through the compassion of a woman who disobeys her father’s decree. Her pity opens the way.
She named him Moses, “because,” she said, “I drew him out of the water.”
Moses grows up in Pharaoh’s palace but is nursed by his own mother, so he knows who he is. God prepares his servant in two worlds.
Who made you a ruler and judge over us?

Moses acted for his people but by his own anger and his own authority, and they refused him. Stephen later recalls these very words in Acts 7:27 and 35. God’s call will come, but at God’s hour and in his way.
ch: The Church has always read the life of Moses as a shadow of Christ. Matthew tells of the infancy of Jesus in a way that recalls this story: a wicked king orders the death of children, the child is saved, and he is brought out of Egypt (Matthew 2). The Letter to the Hebrews praises the faith of Moses’ parents and says that Moses chose to share the ill-treatment of God’s people rather than enjoy the pleasures of Pharaoh’s house (Hebrews 11:23–25). The water that carries and saves is also a sign the Church has loved: the Catechism recalls that the ark of Noah and the crossing of the Red Sea foreshadow the saving water of Baptism (CCC 1219–1221).

set: After sending out the Twelve (chapter 10), Jesus answered the question of John the Baptist’s disciples and spoke of John and of “this generation” (11:2–19). Now he turns to the towns where he had done most of his deeds of power. Chorazin, Bethsaida and Capernaum lay close together on the northern shore of the Sea of Galilee. Capernaum was the town Jesus made his home (4:13; 9:1), and Bethsaida was the home town of Philip, Andrew and Peter (John 1:44). All these hearers were Jews, and Jesus speaks as a prophet to his own people, as Amos and Jeremiah did before him.
str: v. 20: the reproach: the towns did not repent.
vv. 21–22: Chorazin and Bethsaida are compared with Tyre and Sidon.
vv. 23–24: Capernaum is compared with Sodom.
kw: The Gospel’s word for miracles. They are not meant to impress but to call people to turn to God.
Literally to change one’s mind and direction. Repentance is not only sorrow but a new way of living.
The cry of the prophets (Isaiah 5:8–23). It is as much a lament as a threat, like the cry of someone at a funeral: how sad that it should come to this.
vv: Woe to you, Chorazin! Woe to you, Bethsaida!
Tyre and Sidon, pagan cities of the Phoenician coast, had been denounced by the prophets (Isaiah 23; Ezekiel 26–28). Jesus says that even they would have repented if they had seen what Galilee saw.
on the day of judgment it will be more tolerable for Tyre and Sidon than for you.
Responsibility is measured by the light received. The more we have been given, the more is asked (compare Luke 12:48).
will you be exalted to heaven? No, you will be brought down to Hades.

These words echo Isaiah 14:13–15, where the proud king of Babylon wants to climb to heaven and is cast down to the pit. Capernaum, honored by the presence of Jesus, is warned not to make that kind of pride its own.
ch: The Church reads these words as a call to conversion, not as a curse on any town. The Catechism teaches that Jesus’ warnings about judgment are urgent calls to conversion and that God wishes no one to be lost (CCC 1036; 1037). The Fathers often taught that the more of God’s gifts we receive, in the word and in the sacraments, the more we are accountable for them (in substance). For us the question is whether the Gospel, heard every Sunday, really changes us.

qa: Does Jesus condemn the people of Capernaum and the other towns for ever?

The passage is a prophetic warning, spoken with sorrow. It does not say that every person in those towns was lost; many of Jesus’ closest followers came from them. Jesus compares the towns with Tyre, Sidon and Sodom to show how serious it is to receive God’s gifts and not respond. The goal of every woe in the Bible is repentance.
study: Moses’ mother and Pharaoh’s daughter each did a small act of courage and mercy. What small act could I do for a child or a family in danger?
Jesus says that more is asked of those who have seen more of God’s works. What have I been given that I have not yet answered?
